common_name: Čačanska Rodna Plum (Serbian Drying & Brandy Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in early spring; self-fertile and productive without a second cultivar nearby, though a pollinizer can boost set in cool springs.

directions: Bred at the Fruit Research Institute in Čačak, Serbia, from a Stanley x Požegača cross and released in the mid-1970s, this cultivar was developed specifically to combine the dessert quality of Stanley with the drying and distilling tradition of Požegača. Trees crop young, heavily, and with unusual reliability year after year, setting small-to-medium oval plums with firm blue-bloomed skin and sweet, firm yellow-amber flesh that separates cleanly from the pit. Fruit ripens in late summer, just ahead of its sister selection Čačanska Lepotica, and its high soluble-solids content makes it a favorite across the Balkans for prunes and for distilling into šljivovica. Thin a heavy-set tree in early summer to improve fruit size, and expect dependable production even in seasons that stress other plum cultivars.
sources: ResearchGate — 'Čačanska Rodna': a plum cultivar for drying

planting.note: Sow or transplant only after soil has warmed well past last frost; this landrace needs a long, hot, dry season to reach full sweetness.

directions: Obi-Novat (literally 'father of sugar') is a Silk Road-era melon landrace from the Samarqand region of Uzbekistan, now also grown around Bukhara and the Fergana Valley. Fruit is medium-sized with a strikingly mottled rind in bands of green, orange, and yellow, often with a rounded protrusion at the blossom end, enclosing pale green to ivory flesh that turns soft, melting, and intensely honey-aromatic at full ripeness. Because the flesh becomes so tender and juicy when fully ripe, fruit bruises and spoils quickly after harvest, which is why this variety has remained a local specialty rather than a shipping melon. Give vines full sun, warm nights, and let fruit ripen fully on the vine for the best floral sweetness, harvesting promptly since storage life is short.

common_name: Kishmish Vatkana Grape (Uzbek Black Seedless Raisin Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant rooted cuttings in spring against a warm, sunny trellis or wall in cooler climates; needs a long, hot season to size and sweeten its seedless berries.

directions: First documented in the early 20th century in the Uzbek oasis town of Shakhrisabz south of Samarqand, Kishmish Vatkana is one of the oldest named seedless 'kishmish' table and raisin grapes of Central Asia, closely related to the Sultanina/Thompson Seedless lineage. Vines produce compact clusters of small, dark-skinned, seedless berries with crisp, sweet flesh well suited to sun-drying into dark raisins as well as fresh eating. The cultivar is notable in viticultural research as one of the original carriers of a natural powdery-mildew-resistance gene, making it valuable in modern breeding programs. Train on a sturdy trellis in full sun, prune to renewal spurs each winter, and expect berries to ripen late in a long, dry summer.

common_name: Subkhona Apricot (Fergana Valley Uzbek Heirloom Apricot)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring in a sheltered, sun-baked site; this Central Asian cultivar blooms early, so avoid frost pockets.

directions: Subkhona (also transliterated Subhoniy) is a traditional apricot cultivar grown for generations in the garden orchards of Uzbekistan's Fergana Valley, one of the world's great centers of apricot diversity. Fruit ripens to a vivid, saturated orange with firm yet tender flesh and a rich, full-bodied, distinctly sweet flavor that regional producers consider notably different in character from Turkish or Iranian dried apricots. Its dense, consistent flesh holds up well to sun-drying, and dried Subkhona apricots are prized in local and export markets for their reliable size and color. Plant in full sun with excellent drainage, since Central Asian apricot types like this one thrive on hot, dry summers and resent humid or waterlogged soil, and net or cover young trees if late spring frosts threaten the early bloom.
sources: Sunny Fruit — Uzbekistan dried fruit producer notes on Subkhona
FAO — Genetic Resources of Apricots in Central Asia

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring; this landrace was selected for thin, poor soils and a short growing season.

directions: Poljak, known locally as grah poljak, was the traditional staple grass pea of the karst region of Popovo Polje near Trebinje in Herzegovina, grown for centuries on stony, nutrient-poor ground where little else would thrive. Seeds are irregular, angular, and pebble-like, ranging through shades of gray, brown, and speckled tones, and are cooked much like a dried field pea after a short, warm growing season. The vining, slender-stemmed plant needs almost no fertility and tolerates drought far better than common beans, making it a historically important crop in Mediterranean-climate Herzegovina. Sow thickly in a sunny bed with minimal irrigation, let pods dry fully on the plant before harvest, and note that grass pea should always be a minor part of the diet rather than a staple, since excess consumption is linked to the neurological condition lathyrism.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity, Ark of Taste — Poljak Bean

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant out once nights stay reliably warm.

directions: Sanjollas has been grown for well over a century in the village of Sanjollas in Albania's Kolonja Municipality, where local tradition holds that it arrived from Istanbul generations ago and remains a prized local specialty. Vines set large fruit, commonly reaching close to half a pound, with a sweet flavor and distinctive aromatic character that growers in the region describe as unlike other local tomatoes. Fruit is harvested fresh for salads and sauces through summer, and surplus is traditionally sun-dried or pickled to carry the flavor through winter. Stake or cage plants for support, since fruit size can bend unsupported stems, and water consistently through fruit set to avoid cracking on such large-fruited types.
sources: Invest in Albania — Varieties of Heirloom Tomatoes in Albania

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; this variety is noted locally for tolerating cooler nights better than most heat-loving heirlooms.

directions: Known in Albanian as Domate Zemer Kau ('ox-heart tomato'), this landrace has been grown throughout central Albania for roughly a century and still makes up a significant share of local tomato plantings in that region. Fruit is large, pink-skinned, and distinctly heart-shaped, with dense, meaty, aromatic flesh that growers favor for slicing, salads, and cooked sauces alike. Plants bear over a long season from midsummer into autumn and have a local reputation for standing up to late blight and cool spells better than many other traditional varieties grown alongside them. Because the fruit is tender and bruises easily, it is grown mainly for local and home use rather than long-distance shipping, so stake plants well and harvest regularly at full color for best flavor.
sources: Invest in Albania — Varieties of Heirloom Tomatoes in Albania
